utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. For the witness to enter the courtroom, we'll first move into closed session, since there are no preliminaries, as far as the Chamber understands.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning, Witness RM013. I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony yesterday. You'll now be re-examined by Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: RM013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: At page 8928 and 8929 of the transcript, you testified that there were Serb passengers on the bus with you when you were taken from Montenegro back to Foca. Were those Serbs also taken to KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: RM013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they, too, were taken to KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And were they held at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: RM013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see them a couple of days, and then I noticed that they disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Do you know where at KP Dom they were held?

utterances.speaker: RM013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were held on the other side of the -- the room where I was, across the hall, room 20. And I believe that their room was room 16, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And when you say "they disappeared," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RM013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I meant that they were taken to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Also at page 8928 of the transcript, you testified that you were assisted by a Serb neighbour when you fled from Foca to Montenegro in April 1992. Without identifying that neighbour, did the neighbour actually leave Foca with you?

utterances.speaker: RM013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He went with me all the way from Foca to Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Why did he go with you?

utterances.speaker: RM013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were on very good terms, good neighbours. He offered to go with me himself. He could not bear to allow that I -- the thought of me perhaps being mistreated, me or my wife or children.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Did you go through the check-points with your neighbour?

utterances.speaker: RM013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Were there any problems going through check-points?

utterances.speaker: RM013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we went through the check-points, they searched us, and they used all sorts of vial language talking to -- addressing my Serb neighbour, and the -- the thing was, you know, how was it that he was going to save Balijas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And just so it's clear for the record, when you say "Balijas," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: RM013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is a pejorative term that Serbs use for Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Were you able to identify who was manning the check-points? I don't mean specifically the identities. I mean what type of check-points were they.

utterances.speaker: RM013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were military check-points, manned by military personnel. They were in camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yesterday in response to questions by the Defence, at page 8920 of the transcript, you testified about the Red Cross visit to KP Dom. You said, and I'm going to quote from the transcript. For the record, this is starting at 8920.4: "Q. Did you have information as to whether Red Cross, the Red Cross representatives spoke to any of the inmates of the KP Dom? "A. Yes. They spoke to Mr. Rasovic, who was the head of guard. They kept insisting that other people be registered as well. They had knowledge of that group that was being hidden because my brother was in the camp as well and he was registered. And he told the Red Cross that there was myself and others who were being kept hidden there." In this statement, who told the Red Cross that you and others were hidden there?

utterances.speaker: RM013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during the registration with the Red Cross at the time when I was registered, they indicated that they knew that we had been kept hidden away. And I believe I've already said that I -- that my brother had managed to inform them, and he kept telling them that there was a group of people that were being held, hidden, and I was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness gave evidence related to the attack on Foca in April 1992 at page 8916 of the transcript. In reliance upon adjudicated facts 538, and 541 through 548, the Prosecution will not be questioning the witness as to that evidence. For the final question that I have for this witness, we need to be in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Moloto has one question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. This morning, Ms. MacGregor asked you a question at page 4 of the this morning's transcript, line 4, as to the identity of the people who were manning the check-points. Your answer was, at page 4, line 4: "These were military check-points, manned by military personnel. They were in camouflage uniforms." My question to you is: Do you know which army they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: RM013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They belonged to the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also have one question for you. You said that the people who were transported back with you, that you saw them for a couple of days in KP Dom, and they then disappeared. Ms. MacGregor then asked you, What do you mean by disappeared? And you said, Well, they were taken out and brought to the front. Now, how do you know that they were taken to the front? I can understand that you see them to be taken out and you didn't see them any further. But how did you know that they were taken to the front?

utterances.speaker: RM013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were instances where the guards told us themselves. Those who wanted to have anything to do us, they told us. Because these people never returned. They did not come back to KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the guards told specifically about that group, that they were taken -- they had been taken to the front, or that they were taken to the front?

utterances.speaker: RM013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other than that group, there were other detained Serbs, in other rooms, who had probably refused to respond to the call-up and refused to go to the front line, so they had difficulties, and they were held in other -- kept in other rooms. All the Serbs, both from the group that I mentioned and the Serbs that were detained there, they just weren't there anymore. They disappeared after five or six days after we had come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that you didn't see them any further. But did they specifically always tell you where they had been taken?

utterances.speaker: RM013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, later on, from what I learned from the guards, one of the men who had been brought there, he was from Capljina, I was told that he had been killed. And then I put two on two together, that all of these men had been taken to the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any further questions, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a few short one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. RM013, I will just briefly refer you to one of your answers that these -- that there were men in camouflage uniforms manning check-points and that you said that they were members of the Army of Republika Srpska. What period of time are we talking about? April 1992?

utterances.speaker: RM013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 12th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But yesterday we agreed that the Army of Republika Srpska was established on the 12th of May, 1992. In other words, a month after the date when you went through the check-points. Would you agree with me that these people most certainly could not have been members of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RM013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't agree with you because the Yugoslav People's Army was no longer there. The Yugoslav People's Army, its function ceased when the war broke out, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Yugoslav People's Army withdrew from Bosnia on the 19th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RM013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the exact date. I do know that it withdrew, but I don't know specifically when.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that these people at the check-points were in camouflage uniforms. Could you, as you sit here, describe those camouflage uniforms worn by soldiers in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: RM013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these were multi-patterned uniforms. That's what camouflage uniforms are to me. I don't know how to describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the predominant colour was?

utterances.speaker: RM013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was green and yellow and black.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see any insignia worn by these men?

utterances.speaker: RM013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that I knew nothing about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that the Serbs who were in prison, either the group that had been brought there with you or that was already there, that they were all removed from KP Dom. Are you saying that while you were at KP Dom throughout the rest of the period, there were no Serbs detained there?

utterances.speaker: RM013 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, they kept bringing in those who committed some kind of infraction or offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was all I had. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Witness RM013, this concludes your testimony. As far as admission of documents are concerned, we can deal with that in the absence of the witness. We'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I'd like to wish you a save return home again. For you to allow to leave the courtroom, we'll turn into closed session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll first deal with documents still to be admitted. If you would introduce them, Ms. MacGregor, briefly telling us also what it is. I think we start with P982, statement, and P983, another statement, and corrections to the statement, P984.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. You've just identified the three statements that the Prosecution submits as the witness's 92 ter statement and asked to be moved into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, anything in addition to the [Overlapping speakers] objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] We just maintain our objection to P984.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was for the disclosure?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Late disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, is there -- could you tell us already at this moment is there anything you consider that needs further attention or would you rather consider it? Because the Chamber -- if the late disclosure causes seriously problems to the Defence, of course, the Chamber will seriously look at that once it has been brought to our attention in more specific terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because of the man power the Defence has, everything late disclosure to us is really a huge burden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P982, P983, and P984 are admitted into evidence, under seal. Mr. Lukic, if at any later point in time the further exploration of what was lately disclosed to you which was of limited content, it would trigger any need to -- whatever remedy, the Chamber would like to hear from you. Then I think we have two -- P987. That is the chart.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. P987 with the attachment of 65 ter 28723A, which is the corrected version of the chart --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that has been uploaded already and has it already been attached to the chart so that it would make one exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If you can give me one moment, I'll speak to Ms. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, currently, the documents have two separate 65 ter numbers. If you prefer, we can upload them as one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the chart, P987, is admitted into evidence, under seal. And hereby leave is already granted to attach to the chart the new version, which is, at this moment, still separate but could be attached to it. Madam Registrar, is that clear enough?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I just need to be provided with the new 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the last one would be P988, which was ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the list of detained persons. Well, I think it was released ever since but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be released persons. Mr. Lukic, anything ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, do we -- in the meantime, do we have any data on this document? Who created it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because they were provided by an accused in another case. And have you made any research on the background of it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I don't have additional information yet. I have some queries out on a way to find more information about the document and I can make a submission to the Court at a later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait for the results of that. And, until that moment, it will remain marked for identification. Then these were all, I think. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The next witness is Mr. Brennskag. And Mr. Shin will be leading the evidence of that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. If I may make some preliminary remarks while waiting for the witness to come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: The Prosecution may have caused some confusion from e-mails relating to exhibits with this witness and I apologise for that. I would just like to briefly indicate what the Prosecution intends with the exhibits so that there's some clarity now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: The Prosecution intends to address only five exhibits with this witness, pending, of course, any issues that may arise during the course of the entirety of examination. Only one will be tendered as an associated exhibit. The other four we will be addressing with the witness. One of the four is an exhibit, that's exhibit 14178, 65 ter, which we had noticed -- I'm sorry, I'm speaking too quickly so I'll slow down. 65 ter 14178 we had noticed in our 92 ter motion as one we had not anticipated tendering. It's two -- it's two pages, two photographs, relating to a specific location and we do expect to use that in the direct examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So at least confusion most likely is over now. We'll see how to proceed. Good morning, Mr. Brennskag. Not very polite of us, perhaps, to continue talking when you enter the courtroom. Welcome. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brennskag. Please be seated. Mr. Shin, I do not know whether there were other matters before we start the witness's testimony but I didn't want him remain standing any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, there are no other preliminary matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And I apologise as well to you, Mr. Brennskag, for speaking while you were standing there. Good morning, Mr. Brennskag. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: My name is Per Anton Brennskag.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, is it correct that you provided signed statements to the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal in May of 1996 and October of 2006?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And have you previously testified before this Tribunal in the cases against Dragomir Milosevic in March of 2007; Momcilo Perisic in February of 2009; and Radovan Karadzic, on the 29th of October and the 1st of November, 2010?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In preparation for your testimony in the Karadzic case, did you review a statement that amalgamated relevant portions of your previous statements and other information provided to the OTP, as well as from your testimony in the Milosevic and Perisic cases?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, I've been cautioned that we should give a pause between the question and answer to give time for the interpreters to catch up. That's primarily my fault. I will try to keep that in mind as well. And in preparing to give evidence here today, did you have a chance to review this amalgamated statement?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could I please have 65 ter 28710 brought up on e-court. Mr. Brennskag, once the document is on the screen - and we have it now - could you please take a look at the first page and indicate whether you recognise the signature at the bottom to be yours?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And if I could please have the last page of the document on e-court. Mr. Brennskag, I'll ask you again if you recognise the signature at the bottom to be yours.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document to be your amalgamated statement?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Were you able in the course of preparing for your evidence here today, were you able to identify any clarifications that you wished to make to this document? And if you could just indicate yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes, I -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution will go through these clarifications now with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, did one of those clarifications relate to your background as set out in paragraph 1 of your amalgamated statement? And if I could have page 2 brought up in e-court, please. Did you have a clarification you wished to make regarding your background; in particular, your training and education?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. I attended the Norwegian Military Academy during 1971 to 1974.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the other clarification relate to your description of the trajectory of a modified air bomb? And we would like to go to paragraph 34 of the amalgamated statement on e-court, please, and that is on page 10 of the -- of the English and page 15 of the B/C/S. Is it correct that you wished to make a -- that you wished to make a clarification of a sentence in the middle of paragraph 34 where it states: "Then it falls straight to earth." And you may wish to begin a couple of sentences before that, beginning: "The trajectory of such a device is distinctive."

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. When the modified air bomb when the rockets have burned out, the projectile does not, of course, fall straight to the ground but slowly make a curve, almost like a ballistic curve, down to earth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: With those corrections in mind, if you were asked about the matters covered in your amalgamated statement today, would you provide the same information, in substance, as contained therein?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes, to my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And having taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm that the information in the amalgamated statement is truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 28710 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections? Yes, Mr. Stojanovic hints there are no objections. Madam Registrar, the statement would receive number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28710 receives number P992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P992 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: With respect to the associated exhibits, Your Honours, as I had indicated, we would be tendering only one. And that is 65 ter 10159. And I -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Stojanovic, that is photographs of the crime scene concerning a shelling incident, 22nd of June, on Geteova Street Sarajevo. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, 65 ter 10159 will be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P993, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P992 is admitted. 993 is admitted. I made a mistake. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. With your permission I will now read a brief summary of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, a retired lieutenant-colonel from the Royal Norwegian Army was deployed with the United Nations in Bosnia on the 22nd of March, 1995, as a Military Observer. He was initially stationed with the UNMO team in Pale until the 24th of May 1995, with responsibility for monitoring weapons collections points. He describes the heavy restrictions placed on the UNMO team by the VRS. On the 2nd of June, the witness was posted to the UNMO team in Pofalici on territory held by the Bosnian government, where, from OP-4, an observation post in Vikovac, he observed shelling incidents. Although he saw firing from both side, most of the firing was coming into Sarajevo from the VRS-held side. His duties with the Pofalici UNMO team included investigations of shelling incident, patrols, and humanitarian work. Mr. Brennskag describes the intensity of shelling in June 1995, including a 24-hour period when he observed up to 150 impacts incoming into Sarajevo. He describes modified air bombs he first observed in June 1995, which were launched from VRS positions in Ilidza. The witness also investigated incidents involving modified air bombs in Alipasino Polje on the 22nd of June 1995 and another on the 1st of July. The witness describes seeing on 28 June 1995 a modified air bomb that was launched from VRS-held territory and that hit the Sarajevo TV building. He also describes the shelling of the PTT building on the same day. Your Honours, that concludes the witness's evidence summary. If we may proceed to the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Shin. I think the totality of the time for this witness was half an hour, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I would suggest that would bring us most likely just a bit over 10.30, that we try to take the break slightly later and that you can finish your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, in your amalgamated statement at paragraph 18 you state that you marked a map which showed the location of OP-4. Could I please have 65 ter 19747 on e-court. While we're waiting for that, Mr. Brennskag, you had indicated in your statement that you had marked the location of OP-4 with a blue triangle. Just briefly, Mr. Brennskag, is this the map that shows OP-4 with that blue triangle?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. This is -- the triangle is observation post 4 at Vikovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 19747.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19747 receives Exhibit P994, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could I please have 65 ter 19745 on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, Mr. Brennskag, while we're waiting for that, in your statement, amalgamated statement, at paragraphs 49 through 51, you discuss an investigation on the 1st of July, 1995, into a modified bomb impact. In paragraph 49 you indicate that you mark a map with a circle showing where that impact was. Now, looking at this map, is this the map and is that green circle the circle showing where the impact was on the 1st of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: This the map, and it's the mark and to be as far as I remember the place, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have not found a green circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's in the centre to the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I see it. A very small one. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: The Prosecution would tender 19745 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19745 receives P995, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P995 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I could please have 65 ter 14178 brought up on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, while we are waiting for that document, also in relation to the 1st of July, 1995, modified air bomb impact investigation, you discuss in paragraph 51 of your amalgamated statement certain photographs which showed damage at that location. Could you, looking at the screen, first at this photograph - and then could I have the second one please. That would be on the B/C/S version. Do you recognise -- while we're waiting -- yes. Do you recognise these two photographs to be those photographs that you explain in your amalgamated statement?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. This is the Bosnian police photograph, but I have seen it here in court before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Brennskag.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 14178 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 14178 receives P996, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I could next please have 65 ter 09801 brought up on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, Mr. Brennskag, while we are waiting for this document to come up on the screen, you note in your amalgamated statement, paragraph 33, that you were asked in your Perisic testimony about an UNMO daily sitrep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can I just have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: My apologies to the -- to the Court Officer. I am actually looking for 09081. So I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, while we're waiting for the correct document to come up on the screen, this is -- you'll recall in your Perisic testimony you were asked about an UNMO daily sitrep. First, looking at the right side of your screen, do you recognise this document as the one that you were shown during your Perisic testimony?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Turning now to the -- near the top of this document, we see the letters DTG and then a series of numbers to the right. Would it be correct that this line indicates that the report is issued at 6.00 a.m. on the 19th of June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: For clarification, what does the designation DTG signify?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Date, time, group.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. In the middle of the page, on this first page, we see -- we see the subject line. Can we understand that subject line to mean this report addresses events occurring during the 24-hour period of 18th of June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I could please have page 7 of the English version on e-court. And I note that the translation into B/C/S was done in two documents for some reason. So it would be the second translation in B/C/S, second page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you also slow down and make pauses between [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... yes. Of course, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, looking at the right side of your screen, we see near -- a little below the middle the letter G followed by the words "UNMO Sarajevo." Below that, we see the words "military activities" -- I'm sorry, "military activity," and then below that "cease-fire violations/firing incidents." Below that, we see six column headings, and I would ask you to describe very briefly the -- what each of those column heading means. Taking first the one on the left, DTG-18?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not sure if we have the right B/C/S page on our screens. Please check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The B/C/S translation consists of two parts and that of course may create some confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. Could I please have the second -- Just one moment, Your Honour, if I can confer with Ms. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I could have ERN -- for the B/C/S translation, if I could have ERN R0086180 brought up, please. Yes. And if I could have the second page of this document, please. And we see for B/C/S speakers we see on the left, at the top, the -- the same designation, DTG, and the -- the next -- and those are the six heads that we'll be addressing. If we go across to the right from DTG.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's the right page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, you had explained the heading, if we look to the right again, DTG 18. The next heading is location and grid. If you can explain what that signifies, please.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: That is the location of the observation post made in six numbers, grid reference. It means within 100 metres in a map of one scale 1:50.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. And the next heading: "Type of fire."

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: What was fired. For example, [indiscernible] explosions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. And the next line -- heading is "origin."

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Origin, from where it was fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And the line after that -- sorry, the heading after that is "impact in target area."

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It's the impact, where it impacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So that would be where the -- the firing incident -- where -- where the -- where it landed.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And the last one on the right, "remarks," perhaps speaks for itself. If I could please turn to -- have the next page in English on the e-court. And in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first ask what GA stands for, as ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Would that be below "origin," Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, if you know, you see under the heading "origin," the designation GA followed by the word "Grbavica." Could you -- if you know, could you please explain.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but as far as I remember, general area of Grbavica. But I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If we could turn to the page 8 of the English. And if you could just give me a moment, Your Honours, to check the B/C/S translation. Just one moment -- just one moment, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's the top of the next -- of page 3 on this B/C/S translation. Okay. If we --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, on the right, if we look at the line approximately one-third of the way down on the page, that begins on the left 1146B, for Bravo, and on the left we see that entry at the very top on the -- on the B/C/S page, for B/C/S readers. So, Mr. Brennskag, if we focus on that line, you've described the headings. Could you explain, first of all, 1146B, would that be correct that this is an incident that was observed at 1146 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: 1146 in the morning, Bravo. It's summertime, local time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And the next line, OP-4. What would that mean?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: That it was observed from the observation post 4 at Vikovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And the next entry there is 1 EXPL.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: One explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And after that, unknown?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: The origin of fire, unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: After that Dobrinja, and underneath it -- I'm sorry, if you could pause for a moment. My apologies. I am speeding up and unfortunately you may be following me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even when you are explaining that, you are speeding up. You do even that at such a speed. Take your time, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours. I will -- I will be very slow now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, under the word "Dobrinja," we see the designation BP 865564. Could you please explain what that signifies?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It's impact, the impact, marked with grid reference within 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And once again, then, by impact, you mean this is where the projectile landed?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And in the last column to the right we see fired BSA. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It means that it was fired from the BSA area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, one final question on this document, Mr. Brennskag. It says here, "fired BSA," as you just explained. But two columns over to the left, we see unknown. Could you explain how we are to understand those two?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. Normally we were two observers on the observation post, and if we didn't agree exactly from where it was fired, we -- we stated unknown. But we agreed that the area was, for certain, on the BSA side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation, Mr. Brennskag. The final area that I will be asking you questions about regard the flight path of modified air bombs, as you've described in your statement. In your amalgamated statement - paragraph 36, Your Honours - you state that you saw four to six modified air bombs being launched from VRS positions. I would like to ask you first if you could explain to the Court what you see when a modified air bomb is launched.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I see the smoke tail from the rocket until the rocket has burned out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And this smoke tail, is this something that you saw with each of the modified air bombs that you saw launching from Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: When you compare the launch of a modified air bomb from a mortar or artillery shell, what is the difference in what you see?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: For example, a mortar and an artillery gets its power from the initial charge. And then you can see or hear from a mortar, like a poof if you are near enough, and in the darkness, you can see small fire. And then you can't see the projectile. The artillery gets its velocity or speed from the initial charge, and you see a big flame, and you heard -- you hear a bang, very distinctive, but you can't see the -- normally you can't see the projectile during its flight, if it is close enough and then you are in danger, you can hear the whistle of the artillery projectile just before its land.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brennskag. To be -- so that we're clear, the smoke-trail that you see from a modified air bomb launch, do you see something like that with regard to a mortar or artillery shell?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You've described the differences in what you see and what you hear between a modified air bomb and mortars and artillery shells. I'd like to ask you: From what you see can you see what the trajectory is of a modified air bomb compared to the -- the trajectory of a mortar or artillery shell?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I try to explain. As long as the rocket on the modified air bomb is burning, you can see the trajectory. It's almost [indiscernible] depending on the elevation. For the mortars and artillery, you can't see the trajectory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And if you could say, how would you compare the height of the trajectory of a modified air bomb from a mortar or artillery shell?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Of course, it depends on how much gun power you put behind the mortar and artillery piece -- projectile. But normally mortars have a very high trajectory. Artillery, some lower trajectory, but it is a ballistic trajectory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And when you are describing here the trajectory of a modified air bomb, can you -- is that something - just to be clear - that you can see from looking at the trajectory of the smoke-trail?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, I'm told that in your earlier answer there's a word missing in our transcript so I'd like to go back over that. You were explaining initially in the difference of trajectory that: "As long as the rocket on the modified air bomb is burning you can see the trajectory. It's almost," blank, "depending on the elevations." Could you explain that again about "depending on the elevation" so we have that accurately.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: The -- the -- the launch of a -- the modified air bomb, the trajectory is depending of which elevation it will be fired. Let's say, example, 45 degrees, 30 degrees. That's only examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, you are beyond your 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. I -- that was actually my last question, and I, in fact, have only one matter to deal with and that is tendering 65 ter 9081.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, then, do that. That has hereby been tendered. Any objections, Mr. Stojanovic? No. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 09081 receives number P997, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P997 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, we'll take a break. You're invited to follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the time, and I'm addressing you, Mr. Groome. The Chamber notes that on the 12th of February, the Prosecution submitted that it is no longer necessary to call Witness RM175. That is at transcript page 8510. I'd like hereby to ask you that the Prosecution confirms that it withdraws the 92 ter motion of Witness RM175, which was filed on the 21st of November of last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's then hereby on the record. Motion is withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated -- yes, you are seated already, Mr. Brennskag. You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. I would like briefly to go through your statement, and then we will take a look at some documents dealing with events that you yourself participated in. Could we now take a look together at 5992, paragraph 6, of your statement that was admitted into evidence. In paragraph 6 of your statement, you comment on your notes. And you say, among other things, that after the training course, you were, as you yourself said, ill-prepared, and this in reference to the upcoming mission. What did you imply by "ill-prepared for the mission"? What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: What I mean by that, the course in Finland, political and historical and the problems, were fixed or focussed at the Middle East. When I was posted in Balkan, we had no such education before I went to Zagreb. But for the exact job, we were not -- I were not ill-prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go through any kind of training for the current events and developments in Sarajevo and around it in 1995?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. We arrived Zagreb, and we had around one week, ten days, with preparations and education before I, for myself, went to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While you were in Zagreb, during that course, were you aware that there was a cease-fire agreement in place in Sarajevo and around it?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: All I was educated and should know was that it was one or two agreements. It was the 20k exclusion zone around Sarajevo and the anti-snipe agreement. That's far as I know today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to see any of those agreements, to read them and learn about them in this way?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: As far as I can remember today, I'm not sure, but I think no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now let us take a look at paragraph 9 of your statement, so P992, and I say this for the record, Your Honours. And the reason that I'm putting these questions to you is that I would like to -- us to comment on this paragraph, I'd like you to be able to see it before. You say here: "One of the agreements envisaged the withdrawal of heavier weaponry outside the 20-kilometre exclusion zone. Heavier weaponry within the exclusion zone was supposed to be collected at the collection points that were monitored by the UN." And then you go on to list what weapons you consider heavier weaponry. The first thing I would like to ask you is this: If you did not have occasion to see that agreement, who briefed you on what the agreement actually implied?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the witness, in his statement, does not explain -let me see, how do you say it - what weapons the witness considered heavier weaponry. He just told us that certain types of weaponry were included in that category which is not the same. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. And I will read the sentence that I would like to ask him about. It says in, in paragraph 9: "Heavier weaponry included, mortars, artillery, anti-aircraft guns, and tanks."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose can you see that. So my question is this: Could you tell us, please, how you personally learned or understood what was meant by "heavier weaponry" in the course of your mission?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It was told me by the senior team member. And during our inspections of the Weapons Collection Point, I learned to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where it say, "mortars," can you tell me which mortars that term "heavier weaponry" referred to, or did it include all types of mortars, regardless of their calibre?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: As far as I remember today, it was mortars from 80 millimetres and up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the term "heavier weaponry" within the exclusion zone, the 20k exclusion zone, did that include anti-aircraft machine-guns, or PAMs, P-A-Ms?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: As far as I remember, anti-aircraft guns were included in heavier weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell the Trial Chamber, this exclusion zone, the 20k exclusion zone, from a imaginatory centre did it apply to the VRS alone or did it apply to the BH army as well?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: That I can't remember today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you also tell us whether I would be right if I concluded that a portion of that weaponry, of the VRS, was supposed to be collected at certain locations and the portion of weaponry that could be qualified as heavier weapons could remain in areas where it had been within the exclusion zone, the 20-kilometres exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: As far as I remember today, it was an agreement that some of the weapons could be within the exclusion zone without being in the collection points. That's why we also inspected those weapons who were not in the Weapon Collection Points.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What I would like to know - and I believe you can find that in paragraph 11 of your statement; perhaps we can take a look for fairness sake - as you understand this agreement, who was it who determined what was to be taken outside the 20k exclusion zone and what weapons; or what it was that was to remain at the previous firing positions, where they had already been before?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: As far as I can see, two questions. First, those weapons that were in the Weapons Collection Point were not allowed to be taken out of the Weapons Collection Point. Those few or weapons who were not in the collection point, they, as far as I know, was an agreement that they should be positioned or stationary where they were. For example, one explanation for why they were not moved to the Weapons Collection Points were that they were not able to be towed or it was some damages. But that's what -- as far as I know today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on what we see in paragraph 11, in other words, that the UN accepted that those weapons could not be removed, my -- I'm asking you whether you know who it was who would determine what weapons should not be removed from the original, or the existing, firing positions within the 20k exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I don't know who.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry -- I'm sorry to interrupt. But, Your Honours, I think the witness may have answered this already. He stated just a tittle bit above that the weapons -- that they were not allowed to be taken out of the Weapons Collection Points but now the question continues as to who would determine whether they could be taken out or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. I think that's -- what Mr. Stojanovic asks the witness now is: Who would determine which weaponry could stay where it was. It has nothing to do with taking them out from the collection points. But which ones were not even expected to be transported into this Weapons Collection Point. Could you tell us who decided that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understood the question and I don't know who in the UN system who decided it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You already suggest that it was decided within the UN system and not agreed upon by the party, for example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will conclude with this area with the following question: How were you informed about this cease-fire? In the event that a warring faction was attacked by another warring faction, how was it that -- or was it allowed to reclaim its weapons, and how?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: The two questions. How I was informed about the cease-fire. I was answering earlier, I have had informed in Zagreb and when I came to Sector Sarajevo. The rest of the question I don't know anything about because I was not informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, your question refers to a cease-fire, and you -- you're asking the witness how were you informed about the cease-fire. The witness, I don't remember him ever telling us that he was ever informed about a cease-fire. His statement says that he was aware of two agreements: The 20-kilometre exclusion zone and the anti-sniping agreement. He hasn't talked about a cease-fire. So I'm not quite sure I understand your question who told you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Honours, in paragraph 9 of this witness's statement, he states that there were two agreements in force, two cease-fire agreements in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you're right. And then he explains that these are the two agreements, the one about heavy weapons and the other one with sniping. Now, if you ask later a question, of course, you should make -- distinguish between the two if that is the case and then perhaps be a bit more precise in what you put to the witness for him to answer. But the witness said -- did you understand the last question to deal with the exclusion zone for heavy weapons and whether, in case of an attack, a party would be allowed to respond to that? Or did you refer to any sniping events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't refer to any sniping events, but I don't know if it was accepted that use of heavy weapons inside the 20k zone. The only thing I know today is that the -- it was several times breach all those -- all this agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stojanovic, this might guide you as well. This witness mainly comes here to testify about what he experienced, and you're asking him questions about legal matters, such as what would be the consequences of A and B. And it seems that the witness is primarily focussing on what he saw and what he heard and that he can provide us with facts on those matters. Would you please focus on that primarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Can we now have in e-court, please, 65 ter document 14064. We need page 3 in the B/C/S, paragraph 1; and page 2 in the English version. While we are waiting for this document, let me just tell you that these are the notes that the present witness made during his sojourn in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Among other things, you say here that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we now have the English version before us --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We earlier had Norwegian, and knowledge of the Norwegian language by this Chamber is not at a level sufficient to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'm going to read the relevant part.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You say here that: "Some of the reasons for the tragic outcome of the UN operation in the former Yugoslavia in 1995 was, in my opinion, due to the fact that many or, in some instances, all of the criteria set out above were never attained. On top of that, in certain situations, I had the feeling that the neutral party was not always that neutral." Just one question with regard to this: Who were you specifically referring when you noted this down?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Let me first explain. My private notes here were not written down during my time as an observation -- Military Observer. It was written down certain time afterwards. And this is a mix of what I know, second-hand knowledge, thoughts, and opinions. So that's why I can't here in court say who this was. But I had a certain opinion that, afterwards, but I can't confirm it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Stojanovic, let's try to approach this in a way we could expect a witness to assist us. You say: "On top of that, in certain situations ..." Could you tell us what situations just for a fact, you -- in what situations you got that feeling? I'm not yet talking about the feeling. Do you remember such situations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was especially one situation on the top of Igman mountain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- where -- can I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where UN white vehicles were camouflaged by the UN military personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There, you described a situation. You said: "I had a feel that the neutral party was not always that neutral." And do I understand that in describing the situation, you already described the facts which gave you that feeling.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, what we interested in is if the witness has formed any opinions is primarily on the basis of what facts and what situations he formed that opinion. Could you please keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In this same document, can we please focus now on page 12 in B/C/S, first paragraph, and it corresponds to the seventh paragraph on page 10 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Among other things, it reads: "Gradually, I began to perceive that some of my fellow observers from certain NATO countries are engaged in a completely different assignment from the one which was envisaged. Trust in 'The Observers' is beginning to crumble." What led you to believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the sake of the interpreters especially but also for the Bench, which paragraph are you reading from?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat once again, Your Honours. It's the same document, 65 ter 14064.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which page, which paragraph so that we can follow [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 12 in the B/C/S, first paragraph, which corresponds to page 10, paragraph 7, in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, I'm going to read it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You say here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is not necessary. It is on the record what you read. We found the paragraph. Put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question, sir, is: What led you to include in your notes a statement of this nature? That is to say, that the observers were engaged in a completely different assignment from the one envisaged and that trust was fading slowly?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. Again, this is my notes, my thought, my opinion, but I can make a little bit more clear. At that stage, it was big preparations -- this is knowledge I have got afterwards. At this stage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No -- no loud speaking, Mr. Mladic. Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this stage, I afterward knew that NATO was preparing for -- to intervene in the conflict. And I then observed that certain NATO countries observers were used as -- to have more information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just verify whether I understood you well. Did you say you observed that certain NATO countries observers -- did they receive more information or did they share information they gained on the ground with whomever? Which of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The last.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last. So they were not just observing but they're collecting information which they would pass on to their own governments or to NATO or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was -- well, I thought, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You thought that. What did you see? What did you hear? Which made you think this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One example, we had UNPROFOR units inside the theatre, and the -- some certain country observers, they had a lot of meetings to UNPROFOR units HQ, and, of course, they dealed with information for the preparation for the intervene -- the NATO intervene in -- in the theatre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They provided the information gained when acting as observers and they provided that information to UNPROFOR so as to be passed on and be used in preparing interventions. Is that how I have to understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I understood, but I can't confirm it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But what then exactly -- you say, I can't confirm it. Where are your doubts? What did you see that made you believe? And where do you think you had not sufficient information to now confirm it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For example, those camouflaged UN white vehicles on the top of Igman. After --afterwards I know that was a part of the preparations for the intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To say that the camouflaging of UN vehicles was a signal to whomever would prepare interventions. Is that how I have to understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, I just want to know what you mean. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll finish with this question. When you said in your notes that trust in the observers was slowly fading away, were you referring to the Army of Republika Srpska due to the reasons that you just explained a little bit earlier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic is supposed to remain seated. If you want, you can use little notes, Mr. Mladic, and, as you may have noticed, we allow you, when you remain seated, at low voice -- I ask you to remain seated. Mr. Mladic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, please, can I have just a few seconds with my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I asked Mr. Mladic, first of all, to remain seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 30 seconds. Low voice. This is not a low voice anymore. You should stop the consultation. You can use the next break for that. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your understanding, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you recall, I asked you if this statement of yours about the loss of trust was something that referred to the Army of Republika Srpska due to the reasons that you enumerated earlier.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: At that time, we had no observers on the Serb side, BSA side, so I refer to what I know. The trust between the observers and the ABiH was bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right to say that at that time it was General Smith who was at the head of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: That I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we have 65 ter 14064 admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 14064 receives number D238, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at paragraph 23 of your statement; P992. Would you be so kind just to comment briefly what you said in your statement. We have to wait for paragraph 23 which reads in the Post and Telecom building your HQ was housed. And I'm asking you whether at the same time certain elements of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were housed on the same premises or only the officers that you specifically named here.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I try to explain. This is what I in my statement remember, who from the ABiH liaison team were placed in PTT building or had their office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you this because further on in this paragraph you say: "They restricted us or placed restrictions on our ability to do our job." When you say "they," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I can't remember who, but through the liaison officers from ABiH, we were told where not to go. And we didn't have freedom of movement, and every time we had to obey those restrictions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You say that the areas that were off limits for you - for example, the hills north-east of town - in view of the position where you were at the time, were you able to fathom why your freedom of movement was restricted and why were you restricted in carrying out your mission?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I answer the question -- the last part of the question. We were supposed to have freedom of movement and to inspect the activities of the warring parties at that time on the BiH side. We were not able to do that because there was placed restrictions to us. So we were not able to go to the confrontation line on BSA -- on ABiH side, and we were not able to inspect where perhaps we thought they had weapons and collections of heavier weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you know why these restrictions were imposed upon you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at paragraph 26 of your statement, P992, where you say that in the vicinity of your observation post, you saw a 55 tank of Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? With regard to what you said about this tank, I wanted to ask you if you were able to see its movement from your position, whether it left its position.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: From my observation post in Observation Post 4, we did not have directly sight to the T-55. But every time we went to the observation post and from the observation post, we could see the tank. And I myself never saw it was moved and I never heard or saw it was fired from that tank. But it is what I observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to your understanding on the 20k exclusion zone agreement, was this tank supposed to be at that location, and should it have been there?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: That I don't know. Because I never knew about any Weapons Collection Points inside Sarajevo, as far as I can remember today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now look at the next paragraph, where you speak about the fact that from your observation post, you had an opportunity to see that both sides were firing. And, then, in the next paragraph, 28, you say that: "As far as the ABH is concerned, we could observe that ABH was firing from inside Sarajevo, mostly with mortars." I'm asking you this: Did you have any information that, apart from orders, the ABH had other types of weaponry?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: What I saw was mortars. I can only speculate if they have other weapons. I think they have, but that's -- I can't confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And let us now have document D156 in e-court, both versions, in B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which corroborates what ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the Chamber's leave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Madam Registrar, you intervened and it is not on the transcript. Could you repeat what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just said that the document just called, D156, is under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, therefore, not to be shown to the public. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this document is dated 20 May 1995, which is a few days before your arrival to OP-4. Here, the commander of the 12th division of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, inter alia, orders, under item 1, the following: "Prepare a VP for a 105-millimetre H, in accordance with the lasta order immediately, camouflage the artillery piece in the VP sector and protect it against reconnaissance by UN forces." Now by relying on your knowledge of artillery, are you familiar with this designation, 105-millimetres H? What specific piece of weapon is this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just intervene for a moment. We have heard this morning about date, time, how it was put on paper. We have heard about grid references. All matters we have heard 100 of times. So unless this is something else than 105-millimetre Howitzer, it's useless to ask about it because we have had -- we have seen long lists of weaponry, et cetera. So, Mr. Stojanovic, if you have any impression that this witness, who apparently does not know this document, could tell us anything else than that this 105-millimetre H might refer to Howitzer, then it's a superfluous question. But the question has been asked. Would you understand 105-mm H to refer to a Howitzer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's an artillery piece, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And H stands for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Howitzer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what this Chamber has learned over the last nine month in this case. If there's anything -- the witness is not here to learn from this document, but the witness is here for us to learn from what he observed. Could you please keep that in mind when you proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The reason I asked this was because of the following: It says here that this artillery piece should be masked, camouflaged and protected from observation by the UN. I'm asking you, according to your experience, could you say that there were similar situations to this one with regard to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is to say, trying to conceal heavy artillery weapons from UN observers.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: The only answer I can give here is that we were prevented to inspect. And, therefore, we never saw or could be able to inspect those weapons wherever they were. So the -- I think this is my answer here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And does that not already follow from your previous answer that you didn't know whether they had anything else than mortars. That you thought they may have had them but that you just don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, in order to know than weaponry other than mortars are concealed, Mr. Stojanovic, you must have knowledge about them having those weapons, which the witness said he doesn't have. So let's proceed. But what Mr. Stojanovic might want to know is the following: Did you ever receive information about activities aiming at concealing weaponry by the army -- the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Inside Sarajevo I can't remember I got any information about that in my position as observer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and in any other capacity, any other situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course we were told that they had capacities but I can't confirm by myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to refer you to paragraph 29 of your statement, P992, where you state - paragraph 29 - that you could see, had occasion to see, that the BH army often fired mortars from a car junkyard near the PTT building. Would you tell the Trial Chamber, please, about this car junkyard from where the BH army fired mortars. How far was it from the facilities where you were housed?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was just between the Observation Post 4 and towards the PTT building. It was a huge car junkyard, and we could see a part of it from the OP. How far, hmm, I can't remember. But let's say 1 and a half k.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the same paragraph, you go on to say that you had heard that the BH army deliberately fired from a civilian area to draw Serbian counter-battery fire, counter-shelling. Who did you hear these rumours from, that such things were happening?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I heard the rumours. Who I heard it from, I can't remember. It was maybe some discussions during our time in the team, or it was from the PTT building. It was a lot of rumours, so I know that I heard the rumours but I can't confirm anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question about this paragraph is this, you say: "I saw the BH army establish military positions within civilian areas, which is something they shouldn't have done." Could you tell us, could you tell the Trial Chamber where you saw these violations happening? Where specifically did you see that happening?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I can't point out today. The car junkyard was -- this place I saw weapons. They had small staff positions, other places in the town. But where I'm not able to recognise today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could -- could I, nevertheless, ask you to try to remember a bit more precise. Was it -- you said in town. Are you talking about the old town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about what we -- about in the new town. The car junkyard is in the new town, and I maybe have pointed out on a map here in the court another place where we knew -- or I visited a small staff from the ABiH. But I didn't see any weapons there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
