utterances.text: Yes. Could you -- if you say the new town, was it a -- an apartment building where civilians were living, in the cellar, or was it a house, or -- could you remember --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This staff was established in the -- the basement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The basement of ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of a building. And I -- I assume that it was living people or civilians in the rest of the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And was that a house, or was that an apartment block, or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apartment block.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apartment block. Was that by any chance in the Dobrinja area or the Alipasino Polje area, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was east of Alipasino Polje area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Alipasino Polje area, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: East of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how many people were there? You said there was staff, you didn't see any arms. Was it five people, 100 people? Was it ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had a meeting in there. Ten people. They had their personal arms, no -- no heavy arms, no weapon positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Personal arms, long-, short-barrelled pistols, rifles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rifles, pistols, rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Rifles and that was it. Please proceed. Mr. Stojanovic, you may have noticed that the Chamber is primarily interested to know about facts observed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will do my best to go through the facts. I will conclude with this question, referring to this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you say, in this paragraph, that the BH army was not supposed to do this, that they shouldn't have done that?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: During my military education, when we establish military positions also a HQ or a small staff, you should not use civilians as a shelter. In my opinion, then, the civilians should be evacuated from the area, if you needed to be there for war reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps this is a good time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is a good time for the break. Could the witness first be escorted out of the courtroom. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, two matters. The witness proposed for this Friday to come and already to be examined in-chief. The Chamber agrees with that. The Chamber has noticed that the Defence is not yet ready to cross-examine the witness, but to the extent a start of the cross-examination would be possible, of course, that would be appreciated. But the Chamber does not find that we are in any position at this moment to push the Defence in any direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have a statement yet, and we don't have the documents yet so even for direct we have to to -- have those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be able to object -- or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I thought there was an agreement. There was no objection against -- to hear the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just raised with Mr. Shin, I don't know if it is transferred to Mr. Groome that we don't have statement and the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It has, and I have asked Mr. McCloskey to e-mail -- to address Mr. Lukic in an e-mail directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we might hear more about this. Then this is not the final scheduling arrangement but we'll further hear from the parties. That is one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Second, I already inform the parties in a little bit more than 20 minutes from now, I'll not be able to continue to sit for this day. And, on the basis of the conversations with my colleagues, I expect that they'll consider it in the interests of justice to continue hearing the case. But we might take a break of one minute then. Mr. Stojanovic, if you're ready, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I have two questions for you that seem appropriate at this point. One, do you remember that in June 1995 there was intense fighting in the area that you observed?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Excuse me, could you be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Specifically, do you know that, in June of 1995, there were -- there was intense fighting, intense combat operations in the area that you observed from OP-4.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: What we experienced in Observation Post 4, that was a very hectic time, a lot of shelling, a lot of incoming artillery and mortars, and also we observed outgoing mortars from ABiH side. But, of course, we couldn't decide where it -- the impacts were on the other side. As I have stated, as I remember, it could be around 150 impacts inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At any point in time, were you informed that the BH Army had launched offensive operations in order to lift the blockade of Sarajevo? At that point.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: At the -- at the time, as an observer in Pofalici team, I was not informed about this. It was obvious that it was no any agreement about cease-fires, and that's also why we thought was a reason why we couldn't do our job as observers -- or -- as observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: From the point where you were, the position where you were at OP-4, you informed on what you had seen in terms of the use of artillery weapons via radio communication; correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Sometimes by radio communication, and sometimes orally. Because the radio communication was an open frequence, and everybody could hear it; also the warring parties. So sometimes we did it orally with -- yeah, orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At one point, you were wounded at your observation post; correct? And let me ask you: Can you recall what date that was?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I can't recollect the date, and I won't say I was wounded. I lost most of my hearing, and I use hearing-aids today. But I can't recall the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How did you come to the conclusion, or how did you see where that mortar shell had come from, the mortar shell that injured you?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I can't remember now from where. But it was obvious from ABiH, and I think I have explained it before, but it was because we were reporting the grid references of the impacts of BSA artillery inside Sarajevo, and, of course, it was a good help for BSA. And that, I think, was why ABiH fired at those, as a warning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But can you agree with me that you had no information yourself, you don't have any personal knowledge, about whether the Army of Republika Srpska actually listened in on your communications.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Of course, I can't confirm it, but it was an open frequence. Everyone has a Motorola. We knew that Motorolas, from my time in Pale, were taken away from us by BSA. So we knew that this was possible and maybe also interesting to listen at our communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on the fact that the facility where you were when you were injured and that that was in the area of -- under the control of the BH army, you conclude that the BH army actually monitored your communications; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. As -- again, I can't confirm that both parties had possibilities to monitor our communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And my final question about this: If I understood your previous answer correctly, you said that you weren't sure where the shell had come from, the shell that had impaired your hearing. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes, you understood -- understood it correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask for a clarification to the previous answer. You said: "Yes ... again, I can't confirm that both parties had possibilities to monitor our communications." Did you say I can confirm or I cannot confirm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know they had possibilities but I can't confirm that they did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now let us take a look at paragraph 32 of your statement, P992, where you stated something different. So let's try and clarify that. In paragraph 32, in the penultimate sentence - I think in English that will be on the next page, Your Honours - you say the following: "In this incident, the ABiH fired mortars at us from a car junkyard." Does this help jog your memory where that shell had come from, the shell that caused injuries to you?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. Difficult to remember. I've stated that the -- came from the car junkyard. It's a slip of my memory, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And let us just verify, check one inconsistency or maybe that's how I perceive it. In paragraph 32 of your statement you also say: "And, of course," --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I first seek clarification what you exactly meant with "it's a slip of my memory," that do you not remember now anymore, or that there must have been a problem with your memory when you gave this statement. Which --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The statement must be correct. I didn't remember now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I have one follow-up question. Could you see from where you were at the time, could you oversee the -- the car junkyard? Could you see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from the Observation Post 4, we could see part of the car junkyard, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And did you see there a weapon firing? Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember. Obviously must have been the -- from the car junkyard. We knew it was mortars there, and it's fairly close, so first thing we knew it was one mortar shell landing in the garden just in front of us and then, afterwards one into the wall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I'm trying to find out is whether you saw anything or whether you thought this to be the only reasonable explanation of the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Must be the most reasonable explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of the situation. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So I would just like to ask you to tell the Trial Chamber, to the best of your knowledge, how far this junkyard was from the front line, the line of separation of the two warring parties?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to -- to -- to tell. It depends in which direction, also. If I had a map, I would have pointed it out, but from the junkyard to the nearest confrontation line, it must be under 1k. But that's just an assumption now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the Chamber would appreciate if any of the parties would present the map to the witness in such a way that he could mark, if he's able to do that. But perhaps we take a precise map just covering the area so that we have a more precise marking. Mr. Stojanovic, either you, or you, Mr. Shin, certainly will be able to find the -- the map. In what area is it approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The car junkyard is in a straight line from the Observation Post 4 to PTT building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the middle of this distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the mortars there to, let's say the confrontation line, around Butmir the nearest place maybe 1k.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have marked -- perhaps you can use the same map that you marked the observation post. Would you be able to mark on that same map where the car junkyard was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can mark where the car -- where the junkyard was. But I also marked the map where I thought the confrontation line was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll deal with the confrontation lines. But perhaps, Mr. Shin, could you assist me, under which number was the map admitted? Or Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We're just conferring for a second to make sure we get the proper P number. It's the document with the blue triangle on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you assist. Admitted this morning, it's P995 most likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave I believe that's P994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could be. I -- I'm totally relying on ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I gain the impression that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You helped us all out, Mr. Stojanovic. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we will see before us a map that you marked in another case. You marked OP-4. And I would like to ask you -- perhaps we can rotate this. One more -- one more -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think for many persons it is easier to have the north up. So if we rotate back one quarter, no. Any -- now one more further to the right. Yes. Leave it to that. I think this is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- best way of -- could we enlarge it slightly. Witness, could you first tell us whether the place you are supposed to mark, whether it appears on this map, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this map, you can't see the PTT building. You see the TV building, but I don't think you can see the PTT building. But I tried to mark where the car junkyard were. And it may be some -- incorrect somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness has marked it. May I take it you want to tender the marked map, now double marked mark. Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we could just put an AO above this circle so that we know what this is a reference to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. AO. And it is the blue marking at the bottom of the map. And the blue triangle was there already from a previous marking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's a circular marking left to the letter A. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Map marked by the witness receives D239, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D239 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me finish with this question. This area where the car junkyard was, is it situated in a residential area where the civilian population lived in 1995?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: To my best memory, I don't think this was a residential area on this side of the -- the river. Mostly it has been factories. But a little bit to the right, it has been residential areas. So -- but I don't know if there live people there at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me this: Do you recall seeing or having heard that the ABH used to use mobile mortars that were mounted on vehicles and that moved along the line separating the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: No. As far as I know and remember, I never heard about it. We knew that the mortars in the car junkyard were firing and then moving. But in which way, I think -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll try to expedite the process. The document put to you by the Prosecution which refers to an UNMO report relating to the 18th of June, would you agree with me that the majority of the firing of mortars that were established by OP-4 observers and registered by them, that the origin of fire is not known?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I have not studied this report thoroughly, so I don't know. I've just shown this report just to explain what the report is -- the -- how it's made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you can just count in the document and then you know how many of them have an unknown source of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did my own counting, but I fully understand what the witness said. However, according to my calculation, as far as OP-4 is concerned and the 18th of June, it was established that 11 projectiles were fired from the VRS portions, six from the positions of ABH, and that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the last part of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can do it, and we can see it as well. And, of course, there is always the slight confusion about what is in the origin of fire column and what is in the remarks column, because I do understand that any differences of view can be reflected in that column. Mr. Stojanovic, first of all, I have to inform you that the map the witness marked was saved before the letters AO were added. Now, the only marking on the map, apart from the marking from the previous case, it being a blue triangle, was a round or a ellipse or a circular marking at the lower part of the map, and that is what the witness marked. I don't think there's any need to do it again. But AO therefore is not on the map at this moment. We take a break of one minute. --- Break taken at 12.46 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we proceed, if the record can show that the Chamber is now sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis in the absence of Judge Orie, who has just left the court now. Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to finish with this paragraph. I suppose that this document was admitted, and I'll finish with paragraph 32 from your statement and then I'll move on to the questions relating to modified air bombs. Let us just briefly look at paragraph 32 of your statement. And let us solve this apparent discrepancy. You say here, among other things, sir: "We reported the grid references of impact from artillery. And, of course, everyone was listening." Today you said that you only supposed that they were all listening. Now I'm asking you: What is exactly accurate and correct? Did you really know that they were listening in, or is it just an assumption of yours?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: As I said, I can't confirm that someone was listening or monitoring. Of course, I couldn't confirm it. But they were fully possible to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have in e-court 1D802, please. 1D802. I needed the next page. I'm going to ask you a few questions relating to the paragraphs 34, 35, and 37 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just with respect to the document that's been brought up in e-court, when -- and perhaps my colleague was going to come to that, and I apologise if I'm interrupting, but if we could have some information about its provenance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, this is an official web site, weapons and artillery pieces produced by Krusik Valjevo, a factory in Serbia. And it can also be found on the official site in -- of weapons and other artillery pieces sold by SDPR company from Belgrade. This is information that has references to official weapons used, as it says here, in compliance with NATO standards. And the issue here is aerial bombs, FAB 100 and FAB 250, and we're going to have an opportunity to see those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if -- if -- in due course if we could receive the information about the web sites that my colleague has referred to, and then we will -- we'd like to take a look at that. But, for the time being, of course, it has not been tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's not being tendered, yes. And if it does get tendered, are you -- do you have -- are you going to take a position on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. At that time, at this point with the information we have we would probably ask that it be MFI, while we have an opportunity to look into its provenance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Very well then. You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And thank you, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So, sir, what I would like to ask you is this: In your professional career, did you have an opportunity to come across this type of aerial bombs? Did you observe their effects and the consequences of their impact?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I think I have stated this before, but, first, I have never seen this page in front of me. And I am not an expert on air bombs, or improvised air bombs. I have never seen it intact. Never. I only -- only investigated two impacts where it is stated -- we have stated that has been air bomb. I have never in my earlier career, before Balkan, seen or been educated on these kind of bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On what basis, then, do you draw the conclusion contained in paragraph 35 of your statement, to the effect that the said air bombs were something that could be compared to Katyushas that you saw fired in the Middle East?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I have seen Katyushas in the Middle East. I have not seen the launchers. They used several types of launchers. By learning, we knew that they were not accurate. They couldn't pin out where they were going to strike. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And then what led you to make a conclusion that a modified air bomb, as you called them, were inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: By those two investigations. They didn't strike where any military compound or positions were. One I -- one impact was in a garden and the other impact was in the vicinity of Alipasino Polje, in the middle of a paved road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: May I then conclude on the basis of this that you understood that the real target was not the actual target where the air bomb fell.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I -- I -- I really don't know, but as an army man, in -- and what I have seen by Katyushas and I've seen those five, six, modified air bombs, they are not efficient in -- in a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In one of the two events in which you were involved in the investigations, you speak, in paragraph 37 of your statement, and you say that to the best of your recollection you marked the place where the modified air bomb impacted. Can you describe for the Chamber the appearance of the crater that you saw where this bomb landed.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I don't have my statement on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, it's P992, paragraph 37.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we have that on the screen just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we also, with your leave, have a copy of the witness's amalgamated statement for his reference, if that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this would be more efficient and faster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... or are you happy with it going straight to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I would kindly ask the witness also to look at paragraph 49 of his statement because he spoke about this matter directly there as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we finish with paragraph 37. You had referred to paragraph 37 first, so can we deal with that just before we go to paragraph 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, according to what you remember, and you mention here the second investigation of an air bomb impact of the 2nd of July. Can you describe the crater?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: It was a -- it's difficult for me to describe it. We investigated it. The Bosnian police were at the same place, and they also investigated it, and they took pictures of the crater. I assume it was a -- what you -- a big crater. As I remember, my colleague was down in the crater, and it was as high as him, deep as him, he was high. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And to the best of your knowledge, what is your estimate of the weight of the modified air bomb? What would be its size? What would be the size of such an explosive device.

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I'm not able to -- to assume. Because I don't have the -- my report or my colleague's report, and it's 18 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since I'm going to move to a specific event in which you were involved on the 22nd of June, I'm going to put to you only one part of the Defence case, which is the following: We say that the modified air bombs met all the technical requirements and that are placed before artillery pieces. These were tested projectiles, and they had the necessary precision of firing. Now, with regard to your knowledge of air bombs, would you confirm or deny this claim?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I neither can confirm or deny this. I only has stated what I have learned about the five to six air bombs I saw being firing in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just find out. From that position of the Defence that you have just enunciated, Mr. Stojanovic, can the Chamber accept that it -- the Defence does accept, concede that they had modified air bombs?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. The Defence accepts that they did exist. It is in dispute only who fired them and also the quality of those projectiles is questionable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you're not answering my question. My question is: Does the Defence accept that the Defence -- that the VRS had modified air bombs? Not that they existed but that they had them, they owned them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point in time, the Defence cannot accept such a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then I don't understand the Defence position as you put it here. How the Defence come to know that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then just make your -- just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to adduce evidence about the origin of fire and we should provide very accurate data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fair enough. I don't understand what you mean by saying: "We say that the modified air bombs met all the technical requirements and that -- that are placed before artillery pieces. These were tested projectiles, and they had the necessary precision of fire." That is what you say. I'm asking you: Did the VRS have this in their arsenal, these kind of bombs, air bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely not, Your Honours. And you will see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will be very specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in view of what you discussed in the Karadzic case, do you have any knowledge whether the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had modified air bombs in its possession?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I think, as I said then, I had no knowledge that the Bosnian -- that the ABiH had these kind of air bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can we please look at the investigation referred to in paragraphs 39 onwards, relating to an impact of the modified air bomb on the 22nd of June, 1995. To the best of your recollection, was that an impact caused by a modified air bomb or by another type of projectile?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: To my -- to the best of my knowledge, and my remembrance, we investigated the impact, and we found rests or pieces from a rocket. Pieces from a rocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that rocket attached to the air bomb or to a 155-millimetre shell?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: At this time, I can't remember. I need the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, can we please have 65 ter document 10158A in e-court; ERN page 5082. And that's page 9 in the B/C/S. Unfortunately, we haven't received an official translation from the Prosecution, and we have sent this document ourselves to have it officially translated, and with your permission I'm going to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So, sir, this is a document that has a number of pages relating to the on-site investigation conducted on the 18th of July, 1995, on Geteova Street, number 12. It is stated that it was involving an improvised device for warfare whose propulsion structure was based on the rocket motor, Grad calibre, 122 millimetres. Whereas, the warhead part of the projectile was probably a Howitzer projectile, 155-millimetre calibre, HEM 107. I apologise once again for not having an English translation. Does this report refresh your memory of the appearance of the projectile in question?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't find what you're referring to. On my right side, I have ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: On the right side is your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's a different document on the right side. Unfortunately, Mr. Stojanovic says there is no English translation at this stage of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because in my own amalgamated witness statement of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry. Sorry, can you stop talking, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I was trying to explain to you, Mr. Brennskag, that Mr. Stojanovic told us that this document has no translation yet. He is reading to you what he has written on it, and you've got to listen to the interpretation as to what is there. So you're not going to see it on the screen. You're going to hear it here. Can you proceed, Mr. Stojanovic? Maybe if you just read again for the witness to hear what the interpretation is. But before you do, so I see Mr. Shin is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, just a point of clarification. This particular page is not actually part of 10158A. It extends past that, past the ERN range for that 65 ter number. We will see if we can try to locate a translation for it. But, at present, we don't have it at hand because it is not actually part of that 65 ter number. It is part of a broader 65 ter number which is 10158 but, again not part of 10158A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In addition to that, I would kindly ask Mr. Stojanovic to introduce this document. By whom was it drafted, sent? Who is the author? We have no idea because we see only the last page on the screen, we have no idea, the date and all these details which are necessary to understand what you are asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. If can you show us to the first page and explain to us from the first page what this document is. For the witness to understand also.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I believe I've read this. Can we take a look at 101582 in e-court. In B/C/S, that's 5079, ERN -- the ERN range. And this is a document that we received from the Prosecution. This is the first page of a document dated 18th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is the next page there?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... is it number 10158A?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Madam Registrar. Mr. Shin said this is 10158. But it goes beyond 10158A. Are you -- are you disputing what Mr. Shin says? Are you saying that it is part of the A part of it? Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There is only one 65 ter number in e-court. 10158. And not another one uploaded separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I've just confirmed that apparently 10158A was not uploaded as such, so it contains -- it does -- while it contains the B/C/S -- the 10158 remains. Therefore while it contains the B/C/S, we -- it does not contain the English. We are actively trying to locate the English to see if there is an English and see if we can bring it up as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Does it then mean that this document before us is 10158 not 10158A because A has not been uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You understand that, Mr. Stojanovic? So we must strike off the A at the end of the reference to this document. Okay. You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will just recap briefly. This is a document from the administration for the prevention -- for crime prevention of the Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo dated 18th July 1995. And the subject is an on-site investigation on the trace evidence at the site left after an impact of a projectile. And I've quoted the fourth page of this document, which has the number ERN 00375082, where it says that the warhead is probably a 155-millimetre Howitzer shell. But, now, perhaps this will save some time. Let's take a look at P993, the second photo, as forwarded by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I'm a little bit confused. You are saying this document we just saw was dated 18th of July, 1995. The document contained a different date. Not the 18th of -- it was at 22nd June or July; I don't recall because it disappeared from the screen. Can you -- can you give us a clear, correct reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Or, better still, can we have a look at the document again ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Especially page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is 22nd of June, 1995, not 18th of July. Are we talking about the same document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. And let me try to explain. This is a collection of documents dealing with the same event, the incident of 22nd of June, that the witness talked about in his statement. The document that I quoted was an expert report prepared on the basis of documents produced by the forensic experts and based on the trace evidence found on site during the on-site investigation of the incident of 22nd of June, 1995, and this expert report was drafted on the 18th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But this is not what we can see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you see on the screens, Your Honours, is the first official report from the site itself. On the 22nd of June. The expertise itself is -- was done on the 18th of July, and the Defence received this expertise in a collection -- in a batch of documents under 65 ter number 10158A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you take us to the page where the document of July, of the 18th of July begins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And again Mr. Shin pointed out and it was confirmed by Madam Registrar that the document with the letter A is not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Take us to the first page of the document of the 18th of July, Mr. Stojanovic. And bear in mind the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honours. Perhaps then we should go on break now so I can reorganise and perhaps provide a hard copy of this document for you. I have it before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then we will take a break for you to recollect yourself. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May -- before we take the break, may we please move into private session. But the witness is excused in the meantime. We will come back at 20 to, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, how much time do you need to finish with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I tried to find out how much time I've used. I have used an hour and 46 minutes and I have asked for two hours and a half and I believe that I will be able to finish --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] you will be able to finish? Can you finish that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should be able to finish tomorrow during the first session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Brennskag, to have kept you so long. We had some of administrative issues to deal with. Okay. You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the meantime, we managed to regroup, and can we please now have 65 ter document 10158, page 6 in the B/C/S, and for abundance of caution could we have this document under seal. Let us look at it in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not broadcast to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me that at the moment, Your Honours, it would be better if it were under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which means not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not to be broadcast. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We would -- we would -- the Prosecution would like to try to assist with this process if we could, but if we had the specific ERN page number in the B/C/S version perhaps we will in other translation packets be able to find the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm being told that there is English version. And the ERN number is 00375079.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At the moment, we don't have anything on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you get it, Mr. Shin, the ERN number?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We believe it would be page 5 on the English, but when we see the documents we'll be in a position to confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, and I think we have the right page. I'm grateful to everyone for their assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is page number 1 of the document that we have discussed, and, as I said, this is a document dated 18th of July, 1995, an analysis of trace evidence of an explosion caused by a projectile impact, which took place on the 22nd of June, 1995. Can we please now have page 9 in the B/C/S version, ERN 00375082. And I put it to you that, according to the witness -- expert findings, that this was -- can we please look at the previous page in the B/C/S. That this was an improvised device. An improvised device, a Howitzer projectile of 155-millimetre calibre. Can you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, can we look at P993, photograph number 2, and my question is the following: According to your memory -- can we please zoom in on the upper photograph? As far as you can remember, would this be similar to the projectile that you found on the site?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: Yes. First, I have never seen the expert report before today. I have -- I have neither seen or own report since it was made in 1995. I have seen this report with the pictures presented to me here in Hague. And it identify -- it's the report from the Sarajevan police that was investigating at the same time as us, and I recognise these pictures as the same place and the same rest of the projectile that we were investigating.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that you have seen these two documents, in your view, would it be fair to say that this was not a modified air bomb but a modified Howitzer projectile of 155-millimetre calibre?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I have stated what I remember, and it's from my witness statement in October 2010, page 12, para 42. And that is what I remembered in 2010: "The impact was in the tarmac, so the back part of the rocket was standing in the asphalt. We found on-site a tube that penetrated the tarmac with four wings inside the tube I could see the rest of the rocket engine. I estimated that the calibre of the rockets was 126 to 127 millimetre. It was clearly a kind of homemade projectile with very simple modifications."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And would you say that I was right to say that that was a Howitzer projectile, not an air bomb?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I have never seen the expert report and the report, of course, had to stand for itself. What I was assumed -- or remember was what I have newly written. So it may be, can be, an improvised bomb made of a Howitzer projectile. But I can't confirm that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Why I'm asking you this? Now, can we please look again at your statement, P992, paragraph 44 of your statement, where you say -- 44: "At the spot of the impact, we couldn't decide where the modified air bomb came from." Now I'm asking you this. After you have seen these documents drafted by the police of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo, would it be correct to say that that was not a modified air bomb?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I'm not quite sure whether we are making any progress here. Paragraph 42 of this witness's statement explains clearly what he thinks this projectile is. And whether he called them modified air bomb or by another name, it is what he explains in paragraph 42 where he doesn't characterise it as a modified air bomb. He just says: "We found on site a tube that penetrated the tarmac with four wings, and inside the tube I could see the rest of the rocket engines. I estimated that the calibre of rockets was 126 to 127 millimetre. It was clearly a kind of homemade projectile with very simple modifications." That's his description of the projectile. Now whether you call that a modified air bomb or something else, that is the actually description of it. So I'm not quite sure what you are trying to achieve by the question you have just put to the witness [Microphone not activated] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in this same paragraph, 42, the expert goes onto say: "The people who launched these modified air bombs were launching them in a certain direction without knowing exactly where they would land." All I'm trying to is to elicit an answer from the witness about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I understand that. I understand that. And I'm saying even if anybody were to call this projectile a modified air bomb it remains what he explained. It remains to be a 126- to 127-millimetre projectile according to his estimate and with four wings. Proceed, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will not ask any further questions about which particular weapon this was. And now I will move to the issue of the direction from which the projectile came. Could we please look at document 10158A, page 2. And, out of an abundance of caution, I would kindly ask this document not to be broadcast as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: As far as you can remember, did you arrive on the location after the officials from the court and Sarajevo police had come to the scene?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I can't remember anything about officials of the court. I remember Sarajevo police and my own team. And as far as I remember, we were at the spot almost at the same time. But that's 18 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now have 65 ter 10158, without the A, and we need page 1 of the document. 10158, without the letter A. Page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that the page you want, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 4, Your Honours, in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that will be the last question of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. Page 4 and ERN 375077 is the English page we need. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right to say that, at that point, you could not agree on the direction from which the projectile had come?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: No. O Team were not in doubt of the direction from where the projectile were coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether at that time it was established on the spot that it came from the westerly direction 270 azimuth degrees, as the document that we're looking at claims?

utterances.speaker: PER ANTON BRENNSKAG
utterances.text: I can't find -- I don't know this report. But we ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Under paragraph 4, sir. How the offence was committed. Just read that sentence below that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It came in from the west. Azimuth 270 degrees. It landed and exploded in the roadway of Geteova Street next to number 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to answer the lawyer's question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We agree that it came from the west, as far as I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, we've gone past the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Brennskag, I must warn you that you may not speak to anybody between now and tomorrow about the testimony you gave or you still have to give until you are excused from further testifying. You may follow the usher. We'll see you tomorrow morning at 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one clarification on the record. Mr. Lukic, with respect to my proposal how to deliver documents to the place where a videolink would take place, that was just a proposal. There's no guarantee that the court over there will be willing to deal with that in that way. Please contact the Registry and make the necessary arrangements, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We stand adjourned until tomorrow, Thursday, the 21st of February, 2013, courtroom I, 9.30 in the morning. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
